<reason>B offered the stronger comparative case: qualified evidence of sustained relief, acknowledged treatment risks, and lasting harms from delayed treatment. A correctly identified substantial long-term uncertainty, but weakened that challenge by demanding lifelong predictive screening and asserting an inadequately supported treatment-induced “pipeline.” B answered both pressure questions directly and clarified that its case included hormones, not merely a supposedly harmless pause. Its net-benefit argument remained provisional but better supported.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s strongest rebuttal was that high continuation among selected patients cannot establish treatment-manufactured persistence by comparison with adolescents generally. Combined with distinguishing careful assessment from guaranteed lifelong prediction, this defeated A’s main attempt to invalidate the screened population.</best_rebuttal>
